content: The National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP), coordinated by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, has developed evidence-based guidelines for the diagnosis and management of asthma. These guidelines, first introduced in 1991 and updated in 1997 (EPR-2) and 2002, represent a consensus among leading asthma researchers and clinicians. Despite their widespread endorsement, these guidelines have not been consistently implemented in clinical practice. To address this gap, a working group from the Professional Education Subcommittee of the NAEPP identified 10 key clinical activities essential for high-quality asthma care. These activities align with the four core components of asthma management: assessment and monitoring, control of factors contributing to asthma severity, pharmacotherapy, and education for a partnership in care. Establishing an Asthma Diagnosis Asthma diagnosis should be confirmed through a detailed medical history, physical examination, and spirometry for patients aged 5 years and older. Spirometry should demonstrate partially reversible airflow obstruction, defined as a ≥12% increase and ≥200 mL improvement in FEV1 after bronchodilator administration. For children under 5 years, where spirometry is not feasible, diagnosis is based on clinical history, physical examination, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses. Factors such as recurrent wheezing episodes, parental history of asthma, or atopic conditions should be considered. Referral to a specialist may be necessary for complex cases or when the diagnosis remains uncertain. Classifying Asthma Severity Asthma severity must be classified at the initial visit and reassessed during follow-ups. Before treatment optimization, severity is determined based on clinical symptoms, spirometry, or peak flow monitoring. Once asthma is controlled, severity is classified according to the level of medication required to maintain control. Proper classification is critical for tailoring treatment plans and requires access to appropriate diagnostic tools and expertise. Scheduling Routine Follow-Up Care Asthma management requires regular follow-up visits to adjust therapy and monitor disease progression. The first follow-up should occur within one month of diagnosis, with subsequent visits scheduled every 1–6 months based on disease severity and symptom control. Spirometry should be performed at the initial assessment and at least every 1–2 years thereafter. Referral to Specialty Care Referral to an asthma specialist is recommended in specific situations, such as life-threatening exacerbations, failure to achieve treatment goals, unclear diagnosis, or severe persistent asthma. Specialists may also be consulted for additional diagnostic testing, management of comorbid conditions, or when immunotherapy is indicated. Controlling Asthma Triggers Environmental and allergen triggers, such as tobacco smoke, dust mites, cockroaches, and pet dander, can exacerbate asthma. Identifying and mitigating these triggers is essential. Allergy testing is recommended for patients with persistent asthma, and avoidance strategies should be implemented based on identified sensitivities. Smoking cessation and avoidance of environmental tobacco smoke are critical components of asthma management. Managing Comorbid Conditions Comorbid conditions, including allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and medication sensitivities, can worsen asthma symptoms. Healthcare providers should evaluate and treat these conditions as part of asthma management. Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for patients with persistent asthma, except for those with egg allergies. Pharmacotherapy Asthma pharmacotherapy should be tailored to disease severity. Inhaled corticosteroids are the preferred long-term control medication for persistent asthma due to their anti-inflammatory properties. Additional medications, such as leukotriene modifiers or long-acting beta-agonists, may be required for moderate to severe asthma. All patients should have access to short-acting bronchodilators for acute symptom relief. Medication regimens should be regularly reviewed and adjusted to achieve and maintain control. Monitoring Beta-Agonist Use Excessive use of short-acting beta-agonists may indicate poor asthma control. Patients requiring more than one canister per month should have their long-term control therapy reassessed and adjusted. Developing a Written Asthma Management Plan A written asthma management plan, developed collaboratively between the healthcare provider and the patient (or caregiver), is essential for effective self-management. The plan should include instructions on recognizing worsening symptoms, adjusting medications, and seeking medical care. It should be reviewed and updated at each visit. For children, copies of the plan should be provided to caregivers and schools. Providing Routine Education on Self-Management Asthma education is a cornerstone of effective management. Education should be tailored to the patient’s cultural and individual needs and should involve family members when appropriate. Education should be integrated into routine care and reinforced at every visit. Conclusion The 10 key clinical activities outlined by the NAEPP provide a framework for delivering high-quality asthma care. By implementing these activities, healthcare providers can improve asthma outcomes, reduce morbidity and mortality, and enhance the quality of life for patients with asthma. These guidelines emphasize the importance of a patient-provider partnership and the need for ongoing education, monitoring, and individualized care.
